quiz.question: Worldwide, what share of girls of primary school age are enrolled in school?

headline: The Biggest Classroom Expansion in History Happened While You Weren't Looking
teaser: Hans Rosling used to ask this question to audiences at TED talks, World Economic Forum sessions, and university lectures. He asked it to professors of international development, to senior officials at the United Nations, and to at least one room full of Nobel laureates. They all got it wrong. Not by a little -- by a lot. The question concerns girls and primary school, and it has a remarkable property: the more informed people believe themselves to be, the more spectacularly they tend to miss the mark. Something enormous happened to girls' education, and the world's most educated people somehow failed to notice. See if you do better.
metaDescription: About 90% of primary-age girls worldwide are now enrolled in school. 71% of people guess the figure is far lower. Here's what actually happened.
summary: Most people, when asked what proportion of girls worldwide attend primary school, guess somewhere around half. The actual figure is approximately 90%. In the space of two generations, girls' primary education went from a minority privilege to a near-universal norm — and this happened so undramatically that most of the world failed to notice.
nuance: Enrolment is not the same as attendance, and attendance is not the same as learning. In parts of sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia, girls may be enrolled but attend sporadically, or attend schools where learning outcomes remain extremely poor. Secondary education completion rates tell a more complicated story.
aside: In 1970, a girl born in South Asia had roughly a coin-flip chance of ever setting foot in a classroom. Her granddaughter today has a nine-in-ten chance. The grandmother did not make the news. Neither did the granddaughter.

emailDigestLine: From a coin-flip chance to a nine-in-ten certainty: the quiet revolution in girls' education that barely made the headlines.
premiumTeaser: The story behind the numbers involves a Bangladeshi economist who made a bet with the World Bank, a school meals programme that accidentally became the largest social experiment in history, and the peculiar discovery that educating girls reduces carbon emissions more effectively than most climate policies. The connections are genuinely surprising.
b2bClassroomNote: Classroom discussion: Ask students to estimate the percentage before revealing. Connects to SDG 4 (Quality Education) and SDG 5 (Gender Equality). Explore the difference between enrolment and learning outcomes.
publishingNote: UNESCO and OWID data aligned. Nuance addresses enrolment vs learning gap honestly.

learn.title: "I Am Malala" — the chapter on why her father kept the school open
learn.description: The story of Ziauddin Yousafzai keeping his school open under Taliban threats puts the 65% to 90% jump in this chart into human terms. The numbers moved because specific people refused to close doors.

fund.description: Room to Read works on the exact gap this chart does not yet show — ensuring girls who are enrolled actually stay in school and learn to read. They operate in the countries where the last 10% of enrolment is hardest to reach.
fund.impact: £15 = one girl's school materials for a year

act.action: Donate old children's books to a local literacy charity
act.description: Enrolment is only half the story — the nuance section of this card explains why. Books in homes matter as much as desks in classrooms, and most local literacy charities are permanently short of stock.
